title: Polynomial interpolation
subtitle: Given a handful of measurements, find a curve through all of them and read values in between.

sections.title: The interpolation problem
sections.body:
You measured the temperature at noon, 1 pm and 3 pm. What was it at 2 pm? You never measured it, but you can make a smart guess by drawing a curve through your readings. That is interpolation. Given points (x₀,y₀)…(xₙ,yₙ) we find a function p with p(xᵢ) = yᵢ, then use it to estimate values between the points.

Here is a lovely fact: exactly one polynomial of degree ≤ n passes through n+1 points with distinct x’s. Every method (Lagrange, Newton, divided differences) finds the same polynomial in a different form. So through 4 points with distinct x there is exactly one polynomial of degree ≤ 3.

questions.prompt: How many polynomials of degree ≤ 3 pass through 4 points with distinct x?

keynotes: Interpolation finds a function p with p(xᵢ) = yᵢ and uses it to estimate values between the points.
Exactly one polynomial of degree ≤ n passes through n+1 points with distinct x’s.
Lagrange, Newton and divided differences find the same polynomial in different forms.

sections.title: Lagrange form
sections.body:
Lagrange has a beautiful idea: build the curve as a blend of simple pieces, each one switched on at exactly one point. P(x) = Σ yᵢ·Lᵢ(x), where Lᵢ(x) = ∏j≠i (x − xⱼ)/(xᵢ − xⱼ) equals 1 at xᵢ and 0 at all other nodes. It is simple to write, but awkward to extend: adding a point changes every term.

For the points (0,1), (1,3), (2,2), (3,5) the value at x = 1.5 is 2.4375. Compare linear interpolation between (1, 3) and (2, 2) at x = 1.5: P(1.5) = 3 + (1.5−1)/(2−1) · (2−3) = 2.5. The cubic through all four points gives 2.4375, because it uses more information. And Lᵢ(xᵢ) equals 1 at its own node.

worked.why: Linear interpolation between (1, 3) and (2, 2) at x = 1.5.
= 2.5 — the cubic through all four points gives a different value, using more information.

sections.title: Newton divided differences
sections.body:
Newton’s form fixes Lagrange’s weakness, and you will find it easier to use: it is easy to extend. P(x) = c₀ + c₁(x − x₀) + c₂(x − x₀)(x − x₁) + … The coefficients cₖ are divided differences f[x₀…xₖ] computed in a triangle: f[xᵢ,xᵢ₊₁] = (yᵢ₊₁ − yᵢ)/(xᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ), then differences of differences. A new point only adds one term. The value at 1.5 is the same, 2.4375.

Do a small one. Points (0,1), (1,3), (2,2). First differences: (3−1)/1 = 2 and (2−3)/1 = −1. Second difference: (−1 − 2)/(2 − 0) = −1.5. So P(x) = 1 + 2x − 1.5x(x − 1). Check P(2) = 1 + 4 − 3 = 2 ✓. The advantage of Newton’s form is that adding a data point just adds one more term.

questions.prompt: What is the advantage of Newton’s form?

choices.text: It is more accurate than Lagrange.
Adding a data point adds one term without recomputing the others.

keynotes: Newton’s form is P(x) = c₀ + c₁(x − x₀) + c₂(x − x₀)(x − x₁) + …, with coefficients that are divided differences computed in a triangle.
A new point only adds one term, and the value at 1.5 is the same 2.4375.

sections.title: Error and the trouble with high degree
sections.body: More points must mean a better curve, surely? Not always, and this is a famous trap. The error at x is f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)/(n+1)! · ∏(x − xᵢ): small when the nodes are close to x and the function is smooth. But using many equally spaced nodes can make things worse near the ends (Runge’s phenomenon): the curve wiggles wildly. So in practice you use low-degree pieces (splines) or Chebyshev nodes instead of one high-degree polynomial. Avoid one high-degree polynomial through many equally spaced points because it oscillates near the ends.

questions.prompt: Why avoid one high-degree polynomial through many equally spaced points?

choices.text: It can oscillate wildly near the ends (Runge’s phenomenon).
It is too slow to evaluate.
It cannot pass through the points.

sections.title: Piecewise linear and splines
sections.body:
So what do engineers actually use, and what will you? Two practical choices. Join the points with straight segments (piecewise linear: continuous, with corners at the data), or with cubic pieces matching slope and curvature at each point (cubic spline: smooth). Tables of trigonometric values use linear interpolation between entries; drawing programs use splines.

Try the table. sin 30° = 0.5000 and sin 40° = 0.6428. Estimate sin 34° by linear interpolation: 0.5 + (4/10)(0.1428) = 0.5571. Linear interpolation between table entries is exact when the function is a straight line.

worked.why: sin 30° = 0.5000 and sin 40° = 0.6428 from a table. Estimate sin 34°.

keynotes: Piecewise linear interpolation joins points with straight segments: continuous, with corners at the data.
A cubic spline uses cubic pieces matching slope and curvature at each point, so it is smooth; tables use linear interpolation and drawing programs use splines.
From sin 30° = 0.5000 and sin 40° = 0.6428, linear interpolation gives sin 34° ≈ 0.5571.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Two lines to take away.

  • One unique polynomial of degree ≤ n through n+1 points; Lagrange and Newton are two forms.
  • Use low-degree pieces for many points.
